title: Vetoes stalled the UN Security Council twice in a week in 1956; a 1950 rule got round them
body: On 23 October 2026 Hungary marked 70 years since its 1956 revolution against Soviet-backed rule, [Euronews reported](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/23/late-invitations-and-spats-leave-hungarys-1956-commemoration-with-modest-guest-list). That autumn the Suez and Hungarian crises reached the UN Security Council within days, and a veto blocked each: on 30 October Britain and France vetoed two drafts on the fighting in Egypt, and on 4 November the Soviet Union vetoed one on Hungary that 9 of the 11 members backed, the [UN’s records](https://research.un.org/en/docs/sc/quick/meetings/1956) show. A 1950 General Assembly resolution, Uniting for Peace, offered a way round: if disagreement among the permanent members stops the Council acting, the Assembly can meet in an emergency session within 24 hours. Asking for one is a procedural vote, which no veto can block, so the Council sent Suez to the Assembly on 31 October and Hungary on 4 November. There every member had one vote. It called for a ceasefire in Egypt and created the UN’s first peacekeeping force, but its call for Soviet forces to leave Hungary was ignored: the Assembly can recommend, not compel.

slides.prompt: On 4 November 1956, 9 of the 11 members of the UN Security Council voted for a draft resolution on Hungary. Was it adopted?
slides.answer: No: the Soviet Union, a permanent member, vetoed it.
slides.detail: At the same meeting the Council voted 10 to 1 to send the matter to the General Assembly. That was a procedural vote, so the Soviet no did not count as a veto.

slides.alt: Animation on ink-blue night: the Hungarian flag with a hole; dates of 1956; the 11 chairs of the UN Security Council with gold rings for the 5 permanent members; VETOED and ADOPTED stamps over 7–2 and 10–1 tallies; the Uniting for Peace text; Assembly votes of 64–5, 57–0 and 50–8.

slides.prompt: Find votes that block a decision with a veto, yet still send the matter to the General Assembly.
slides.takeaway: Seven yes votes and one permanent member’s no do it, as on 4 November 1956: that no is a veto on a decision, but not on the procedural vote that calls the Assembly.

slides.heading: Two crises at the UN, autumn 1956

events.text: Britain and France veto on Suez
A procedural vote sends Suez to the Assembly
Soviet veto on Hungary; it goes to the Assembly
Assembly sets up a UN Emergency Force

slides.heading: Two bodies of the United Nations

left.label: Security Council, 1956
left.text: 11 members, 5 of them permanent. A decision needs 7 votes and no permanent member against; a procedural vote needs only the 7.

right.label: General Assembly
right.text: Every member has one vote and none has a veto. Under Uniting for Peace it can meet within 24 hours, but it can only recommend.

slides.question: Why could Britain and France not stop the UN Security Council from sending the Suez crisis to the General Assembly in 1956?
slides.explanation: Procedural votes needed 7 of the 11 members and could not be vetoed. On 31 October 1956 the vote was 7 to 2, with Britain and France against and 2 abstentions.

source.label: United Nations: Emergency special sessions of the General Assembly
